entry.title: A Replay Ledger for REST Email Verification
entry.summary: Email verification looks like a small feature: create a token, send a message, and accept the link. In a backend service, it is a stateful authentication workflow with retries, expiry, duplicate requests, and untrusted delivery infrastructure. Treating it as only an email-sending problem makes the REST API harder to reason about. The result are familiar: a link works twice, a delayed message verifies an old account, or a retry creates several valid tokens. A replay ledger gives the service one durable place to answer a simple question: what happened to this verification attempt? A verification request usually crosses four boundaries: The client asks the REST API to start verification. The API records an attempt and queues a message. A mail provider delivers a link to a mailbox. The client …

entry.title: Keeping DeepTutor's Local Inference Alive Past the Twelfth Turn
entry.summary:
Keeping DeepTutor's Local Inference Alive Past the Twelfth Turn
The page landed at 3:12 a.m. vLLM in front of DeepTutor had been OOM-killed on turn twelve of a calculus session, and the restart threw away the thread that lesson had just built. The weights were fine. The KV cache was not. I integrate HKUDS/DeepTutor from the outside. I do not maintain the graph. The point of the stack is a lifelong loop: student state, skill traces, and a planner that still knows what the learner missed last week. The model call is a replaceable backend. The failure is inference quietly exhausting GPU memory because the KV cache was sized for a demo and left up across real lessons. A 70B at Q4 or AWQ fits two 48 GB cards until you preallocate a 32k cache and let sessions pile up prefixes that never repeat…

entry.title: The Mathematics of Misreading a Poem
entry.summary:
There is a particularly interesting inconvenience in using your own poetry as a machine learning dataset: you know what the words were supposed to mean. Whether they actually convey that meaning is a different question entirely. I recently decided to turn twelve of my poems into numerical vectors and investigate what happened to the relationships between them. It began as a fairly innocent exercise in curiosity and ended up making me reconsider how I evaluate semantic retrieval systems. entry.title: The 3 AM burst pipe test: where an AI agent should stop and a human should take over
entry.summary: A burst pipe at 3 AM is a useful test case for any AI agent you put in front of customers. The agent can handle almost every step around the problem. It cannot do the one step that matters: someone has to go to the house and fix it. That makes the handoff the most important piece of the design, and it is usually the least specified. I run EGA Futura, a native ERP on Salesforce, and co-founded Vantegrate, an AI agent company, with Francisco Morales. In a LinkedIn post I wrote in Spanish today, I noted that AI now writes code, analyzes contracts and builds apps, while a broken pipe in the middle of the night still needs a person who shows up. For engineers, that sentence becomes a requirement: design the agent so the human who shows up gets everything they need, and nothing the agent guessed…

entry.title: Architecting Zero-Knowledge Anonymity: Building a Safe, Bullying-Free Confession Platform
entry.summary: In the mid-2010s, anonymous social platforms like Whisper and Yik Yak captured tens of millions of users. They promised an unfiltered digital void where people could admit their deepest regrets, mental health battles, and campus secrets without the burden of their real-world identities.
